entries.test: Public estimates of usable training data and model training requirements would show whether AI companies were approaching exhaustion of available data in April 2024.
Published training methods and evaluations would show whether generative AI can improve beyond its April 2024 capabilities without exceeding the high-quality data then available.

entries.note: Calling the approach a terrible idea is an evaluation.

entries.test: Controlled training studies comparing models trained with substantial model-generated content against suitable baselines would show whether that content provides benefits or causes degradation.
entries.note: The proposition drops the qualification that models are fed reams of generated content.

entries.test: Public model research and evidence of AI-related changes in human content production would test both dependence on training data and suppression of its creation.

entries.note: “I'd bet money” expresses a conjecture here, following the explicit suggestion that companies may already have trained on the data.

entries.test: Public licensing terms, publisher production figures, and training-data availability would show whether licensing increases content production and alleviates the asserted shortage.

entries.note: The recommendation specifies funding as many outlets as possible and directly incentivizing reporting; the proposition weakens those prescriptions.

entries.test: Published visual-model experiments would show whether errors can decrease without substantially more data, while dataset surveys would establish relative visual-data availability.
entries.note: Declining to promise a fix does not assert that fixing errors is impossible. The source also compares visual-data availability with text rather than simply declaring scarcity.

entries.test: Public experiments on smaller models trained with limited synthetic datasets would show whether that approach resolves the asserted training-data constraint.
entries.note: The source addresses smaller models trained on limited synthetic datasets; the proposition broadens this to synthetic data and smaller models generally.

entries.test: Public AI valuations, investment flows, revenues, earnings, and subsequent repricing would test whether April 2024 investment reflected a speculative bubble.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives bubble a financial reading.
“Likely” qualifies the explanation for the article's vagueness, rather than directly qualifying Stargate's theoretical status.

entries.test: Public financial results showing AI-related profits at any non-infrastructure company as of April 2024 would refute the exclusivity claim.
entries.note: The claim concerns profits from the contemporary AI boom.
“May not” expressly leaves the financial outcome uncertain.

entries.test: Public investment agreements, cloud commitments, or financial disclosures would establish whether Anthropic guaranteed Google and AWS annual revenue of $750 million and $800 million respectively.
entries.note: Zitron asserts this in his own voice while crediting a source. The proposition introduces “about,” which the stated figures do not contain.
“Not exciting” is a judgment of significance. The proposition also changes his stated 6% of growth into six percentage points.
The proposition removes “I fear” and turns a feared explanation into an unqualified assertion.

entries.test: Public company results, AI infrastructure spending, and cloud-provider revenue disclosures would test the asserted concentration of benefits and expansion despite limited AI revenue.
entries.note: The proposition drops the assertion that every major cloud provider reports little AI revenue and broadens the contextual financial meaning of benefit.

entries.test: Representative business adoption surveys and documented production deployments available in April 2024 would show whether evidence of actual adoption was limited.
entries.note: The proposition turns “I am seeing little evidence” into an unrestricted claim about the evidence available.

entries.test: Public hallucination evaluations, business incidents, and experiments reducing hallucinations without additional compute would test the asserted risks and exclusive remedy.
entries.note: The source specifies more compute to process data, not necessarily more data, and also asserts that AI is destroying the data resource.

entries.test: Public revenue and profit figures for the named AI companies and industry would establish whether high revenues coincided with losses in April 2024.
entries.note: The quoted passage says coverage of OpenAI and Anthropic omits profits; that alone does not assert that both companies lack profits.
The future's failure to arrive is presented as a possibility.

entries.test: Public launch outcomes, sustained commercial adoption, and operating economics would show whether Sora and comparable video models fail commercially on arrival.
entries.note: In context, “dead on arrival” predicts commercial failure rather than merely insulting the products. Public launches have occurred by the evaluation date.
Both the profitability assessment and the prospect of improvement are explicitly uncertain.

entries.test: Public AI demand figures, investor demands, and market reactions would show whether a demand shortfall prompts a revenue-driven backlash against the three firms.
entries.note: The source corrects its antecedent from slowing adoption to demand failing to arrive.

entries.test: Documented generative AI applications available by April 2024 would show whether they delivered materially new capabilities beyond fundraising and publicity.

entries.note: He presents the cascade as a feared scenario, not an unconditional prediction.
The cascade is explicitly only likely. The accompanying claim about required data and compute is independently testable if extracted separately.

entries.test: Public enterprise adoption figures, market reactions, restructuring announcements, and layoff totals would show whether failed core adoption and a market reversal produce tens of thousands of job cuts.
entries.note: The source separately conditions the severe cutbacks on the market turning; the proposition collapses that condition into an assured consequence of weak adoption.

entries.test: Public AI profitability figures and Nvidia order disclosures would show whether failure to deliver meaningful customer and provider profits produces a dramatic order slowdown.
entries.note: The source's firm conditional order forecast is testable. The proposition additionally makes Nvidia's tentative canary role a consequence of that slowdown.

entries.test: Public financial results and market declines would show whether cloud giants suffer substantially worse financial setbacks after Nvidia falls first.
entries.note: The proposition drops “first” from its antecedent, although the separate conditions field retains it.
The passage does not identify a sufficiently definite set of Altman's promises to test impossibility consistently. Ultimate impossibility is also hedged.

entries.test: Public data-generation and model-training results, together with evidence of generative AI profitability outside Nvidia available at publication, would test both assertions.
entries.note: The profitability clause concerns the evidence then available, rather than firmly predicting that nobody else will ever profit.

entries.test: Public power, cooling, and compute constraints and their documented effects on model development would show whether physical limits were impeding further AI progress.
entries.note: “Are blocking” strengthens “reaching the point” and “getting in the way.” The separate description of current AI as mediocre is a value judgment.

entries.test: A generative AI product breakthrough producing sustained mass adoption and a major change in everyday technology use would refute the prediction.
entries.note: The plain contextual reading is a transformative mass-market breakthrough; no deadline is given.
